scenes.narration: How do you know your function still works after you change it? You test it, automatically.

scenes.onScreen: "Check before you ship": three numbered lines (1. assert stops the program if a claim is false; 2. unittest groups checks into test methods; 3. pytest needs only plain functions and assert) and an analogy card: a quality stamp on every function: tick if it behaves, cross if it does not, before it reaches the customer
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: A test is code that checks your code. The simplest tool is assert. Write assert, then a claim. If the claim is False, Python raises an AssertionError. The unittest module in the standard library groups checks into a class, with methods whose names start with test. Another tool, pytest, needs only plain functions and assert, and is very popular. Think of a quality stamp on every function. Tick if it behaves, cross if it does not.

scenes.onScreen: A row of test cards; passing ones get a green tick, a failing one gets a red cross and a message
scenes.animation: Test cards flip one by one; green ticks pop on most, one red cross with a message bubble appears
scenes.narration: Here is the idea of a test run. Each test is a small card with a claim. The runner flips every card. If the claim is true, it gets a green tick. If not, a red cross, and the message. After every change to your code, you run all the cards again, in a second. If something that worked yesterday breaks today, you see a red cross at once, before your users do.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: assert on floats
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the Python error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. We assert that point one plus point two equals point three. It fails. Assertion error, with no message. Computers store decimals as tiny approximations, and the sum is point three, followed by a long tail ending in four. Compare floats with math dot is close instead. It allows a tiny difference.

props.why: Computers store most decimals as tiny approximations, so equal-looking numbers may differ in the last digits. Compare floats with math.isclose, not with equals.

shorts.title: What is a test
shorts.hook: "A test is code that checks your code."
shorts.script: A test is code that checks your code. After every change, you run your tests, and see at once if something broke. The simplest tool is assert. Write assert and a claim. If the claim is false, Python stops with an assertion error. Try it in your own file and watch what happens. Pause the video and type it out yourself. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Tests check your code.

shorts.title: unittest
shorts.hook: "The unittest module is built into Python."
shorts.script: The unittest module is built into Python. Write a class that extends TestCase. Each method that starts with test is one test. Use assert equal to compare an answer with what you expect. Run them all in one go. Pause the video and type it out yourself. Say it out loud once. Then you remember it. Then run it, and compare with what you predicted. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: unittest is built in.

shorts.title: pytest
shorts.hook: "Pytest is a popular tool you install with pip."
shorts.script: Pytest is a popular tool you install with pip. A test is a plain function, with a plain assert. No class needed. Name your file starting with test, and run pytest in the terminal. It finds every test and shows green or red. Say it out loud once. Then you remember it. Then run it, and compare with what you predicted. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Pytest keeps it short.

shorts.title: Float trap
shorts.script: Here is a trap. Assert point one plus point two equals point three, and it fails. Decimals are stored as tiny approximations. The sum has a long tail. Use math dot is close, which allows a tiny difference. Then run it, and compare with what you predicted. Try it in your own file and watch what happens. Pause the video and type it out yourself. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Never compare floats with equals.

shorts.hook: "Why did the test pass the interview?"
shorts.script: Why did the test pass the interview? It always checked its assertions. Your challenge. Write a function called double. Then write an assert that proves double of four is eight.
